claim: Neutrophils are essential for host defense against Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus).
source: Neutrophils are essential for host defense against Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental data provided in this statement.

claim: The neuro-repellent, SLIT2, potently inhibits neutrophil chemotaxis.
source: The neuro-repellent, SLIT2, potently inhibits neutrophil chemotaxis, and might, therefore, be expected to impair antibacterial responses.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract, drawing from prior research.

claim: Neutrophils exposed to the N-terminal SLIT2 (N-SLIT2) fragment kill extracellular S. aureus more efficiently.
source: We report here that, unexpectedly, neutrophils exposed to the N-terminal SLIT2 (N-SLIT2) fragment kill extracellular S. aureus more efficiently.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: N-SLIT2 amplifies reactive oxygen species production in response to S. aureus by activating p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase.
source: N-SLIT2 amplifies reactive oxygen species production in response to the bacteria by activating p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase that in turn phosphorylates NCF1, an essential subunit of the NADPH oxidase complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1E-F and Figure 2.

claim: p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase phosphorylates NCF1, an essential subunit of the NADPH oxidase complex.
source: N-SLIT2 amplifies reactive oxygen species production in response to the bacteria by activating p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase that in turn phosphorylates NCF1, an essential subunit of the NADPH oxidase complex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B demonstrating NCF1 phosphorylation.

claim: N-SLIT2 enhances the exocytosis of neutrophil secondary granules.
source: N-SLIT2 also enhances the exocytosis of neutrophil secondary granules.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In a murine model of S. aureus skin and soft tissue infection (SSTI), local SLIT2 levels fall initially but increase subsequently, peaking at 3 days after infection.
source: In a murine model of S. aureus skin and soft tissue infection (SSTI), local SLIT2 levels fall initially but increase subsequently, peaking at 3 days after infection.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The neutralization of endogenous SLIT2 worsens SSTI.
source: Of note, the neutralization of endogenous SLIT2 worsens SSTI.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: S. aureus is a commensal bacterium as well as a skillful, facultative pathogen causing diverse human diseases ranging from localized SSTI to life-threatening disseminated sepsis.
source: Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) is a commensal bacterium as well as a skillful, facultative pathogen causing diverse human diseases ranging from localized SSTI to life-threatening disseminated sepsis (Krismer et al., 2017; Lowy, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neutrophils form a formidable first-line of defense against S. aureus invasion and spread.
source: Neutrophils, the most abundant subset of leukocytes in circulation, form a formidable first-line of defense against S. aureus invasion and spread (Guerra et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Patients with neutropenia and defective neutrophil functions are highly susceptible to recurrent and more severe S. aureus infections.
source: Accordingly, patients with neutropenia and defective neutrophil functions are highly susceptible to recurrent and more severe S. aureus infections (Buvelot et al., 2017; Donadieu et al., 2011; Neehus et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Infections caused by antibiotic-resistant strains of S. aureus have been steadily increasing worldwide.
source: Infections caused by antibiotic-resistant strains of S. aureus have been steadily increasing worldwide, suggesting that strategies to enhance the effective recruitment of neutrophils and their inherent bactericidal properties are needed to combat the morbidity and mortality associated with S. aureus infections (Chambers and Deleo, 2009; Jernigan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: mRNA encoding Slit guidance ligand 2 (SLIT2) is locally upregulated during S. aureus-induced mastitis.
source: A recent transcriptomic study noted that mRNA encoding Slit guidance ligand 2 (SLIT2), a canonical neuro-repellent, is locally upregulated during S. aureus-induced mastitis (Günther et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SLIT1 is exclusively expressed in the nervous system.
source: Among the three mammalian SLIT family members, SLIT1 is exclusively expressed in the nervous system (Wu et al., 2001), while SLIT2 and SLIT3 are also detected outside the nervous system (Bhosle et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SLIT2 and SLIT3 are detected outside the nervous system.
source: Among the three mammalian SLIT family members, SLIT1 is exclusively expressed in the nervous system (Wu et al., 2001), while SLIT2 and SLIT3 are also detected outside the nervous system (Bhosle et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SLIT2 inhibits directed neutrophil migration in vitro as well as in vivo.
source: We and others have previously reported that SLIT2 inhibits directed neutrophil migration in vitro as well as in vivo (Chaturvedi et al., 2013; Tole et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2001; Ye et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature including the authors' own work.

claim: The cleaved N-terminal fragment of SLIT2, N-SLIT2, acts via its receptor, Roundabout guidance receptor 1 (ROBO1), to attenuate inflammasome activation in macrophages by inhibiting macropinocytosis.
source: We also showed that the cleaved N-terminal fragment of SLIT2, N-SLIT2, acts via its receptor, Roundabout guidance receptor 1 (ROBO1), to attenuate inflammasome activation in macrophages by inhibiting macropinocytosis (Bhosle et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Primary human and murine neutrophils express ROBO1.
source: Additionally, we and others previously reported that primary human and murine neutrophils express ROBO1 (Rincón et al., 2018; Tole et al., 2009; Ye et al., 2010), but not ROBO2 (Rincón et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature including the authors' own work.

claim: Primary human and murine neutrophils do not express ROBO2.
source: Additionally, we and others previously reported that primary human and murine neutrophils express ROBO1 (Rincón et al., 2018; Tole et al., 2009; Ye et al., 2010), but not ROBO2 (Rincón et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Administration of N-SLIT2 in vivo does not confer increased susceptibility to bacterial infections.
source: Despite the inhibitory actions of N-SLIT2 on chemotaxis and macropinocytosis in innate immune cells, administration of N-SLIT2 in vivo does not confer increased susceptibility to bacterial infections (Chaturvedi et al., 2013; London et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Incubation of primary human neutrophils with bioactive N-SLIT2, but not inactive N-SLIT2ΔD2, significantly reduced extracellular S. aureus as early as 30 min.
source: Incubation of primary human neutrophils with bioactive N-SLIT2, but not inactive N-SLIT2ΔD2 which lacks the ROBO1/2-binding D2 LRR domain (Patel et al., 2012), significantly reduced extracellular S. aureus as early as 30 min (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: N-SLIT2 did not affect the ability of human neutrophils to phagocytose S. aureus.
source: Intriguingly, N-SLIT2 did not affect the ability of human neutrophils (Figure 1B–D) or RAW264.7 murine macrophages to phagocytose S. aureus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: N-SLIT2 did not affect the ability of RAW264.7 murine macrophages to phagocytose S. aureus.
source: Intriguingly, N-SLIT2 did not affect the ability of human neutrophils (Figure 1B–D) or RAW264.7 murine macrophages to phagocytose S. aureus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: DPI partially restored extracellular bacterial survival in the presence of N-SLIT2.
source: To determine whether N-SLIT2 decreased bacterial survival by stimulating phagocyte ROS production, a process dependent on NADPH oxidase complex (NOX) activity, we incubated neutrophils with the pan-NOX-inhibitor, diphenyleneiodonium chloride (DPI). DPI partially restored extracellular bacterial survival in the presence of N-SLIT2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Human neutrophils co-incubated with bio-active N-SLIT2 and S. aureus produced significantly more extracellular ROS than S.aureus-exposed neutrophils incubated with vehicle or N-SLIT2ΔD2.
source: Surprisingly, human neutrophils co-incubated with bio-active N-SLIT2 and S. aureus produced significantly more extracellular ROS than S.aureus-exposed neutrophils incubated with vehicle or N-SLIT2ΔD2 (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: Neutrophils exposed to PMA produced more extracellular ROS in the presence of N-SLIT2 compared to N-SLIT2ΔD2.
source: We found that neutrophils exposed to another secondary ROS-inducing stimulus, namely phorbol-12-myristate-13-acetate (PMA), also produced more extracellular ROS in the presence of N-SLIT2 compared to N-SLIT2ΔD2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The effect of N-SLIT2 to enhance extracellular ROS production by S. aureus-exposed neutrophils is not species-specific.
source: Similar observations were also noted for mouse bone marrow-derived neutrophils (BMDN) indicating that the effect of N-SLIT2 to further enhance extracellular ROS production by S. aureus-exposed neutrophils is not species-specific (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: N-ROBO1 fully blocked the ability of N-SLIT2 to boost extracellular ROS production in neutrophils exposed to S. aureus.
source: To determine whether the observed effects of N-SLIT2 occurred through the canonical ROBO1 receptor, we pre-incubated N-SLIT2 with the soluble N-terminal fragment of the ROBO1 receptor (N-ROBO1). N-ROBO1 fully blocked the ability of N-SLIT2 to boost extracellular ROS production in neutrophils exposed to S. aureus (Figure 1G–H).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: Activation of Rac GTPases is essential for optimal NOX function in neutrophils.
source: Since activation of Rac GTPases is essential for optimal NOX function in neutrophils (Diebold and Bokoch, 2001; Hordijk, 2006), we next tested the effects of N-SLIT2 on Rac.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: N-SLIT2 alone failed to activate Rac but instead required a second stimulus, namely S. aureus.
source: N-SLIT2 alone failed to activate Rac but instead required a second stimulus, namely S. aureus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: N-SLIT2 increased phosphorylation of the conserved Ser345 residue of NCF1 in neutrophils.
source: We found that N-SLIT2 increased phosphorylation of the conserved Ser345 residue of NCF1 in neutrophils (Figure 2A–B), as well as in RAW264.7 macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: N-SLIT2 increased phosphorylation of the conserved Ser345 residue of NCF1 in RAW264.7 macrophages.
source: We found that N-SLIT2 increased phosphorylation of the conserved Ser345 residue of NCF1 in neutrophils (Figure 2A–B), as well as in RAW264.7 macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: SLIT2-ROBO2 signaling activates NOX function in neurons by activating protein kinase C (PKC).
source: As SLIT2-ROBO2 signaling was recently reported to activate NOX function in neurons by activating protein kinase C (PKC) (Terzi et al., 2021), we examined the effects of N-SLIT2 on PKC activation in neutrophils.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: N-SLIT2 did not induce phosphorylation of PKC in neutrophils.
source: N-SLIT2 did not induce phosphorylation of PKC in neutrophils (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: SLIT2 orthologues activate p38 MAPK signaling in Xenopus and C. elegans neurons.
source: SLIT2 orthologues have been reported to activate p38 MAPK signaling in Xenopus and C. elegans neurons (Campbell and Okamoto, 2013; Piper et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The p38 MAP kinases phosphorylate NCF1 at the Ser345 residue to mediate NOX priming.
source: The p38 MAP kinases are also known to phosphorylate NCF1 at the Ser345 residue to mediate NOX priming (Dang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: N-SLIT2 potently induced p38 MAPK activation in neutrophils.
source: N-SLIT2 potently induced p38 MAPK activation in both neutrophils (Figure 2C–D) and macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: N-SLIT2 potently induced p38 MAPK activation in macrophages.
source: N-SLIT2 potently induced p38 MAPK activation in both neutrophils (Figure 2C–D) and macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G-H.

claim: Incubation with two distinct pharmacologic inhibitors of p38 MAPKs blocked the observed N-SLIT2-induced increase in extracellular ROS in neutrophils exposed to S. aureus.
source: Congruent with these results, incubation with two distinct pharmacologic inhibitors of p38 MAPKs blocked the observed N-SLIT2-induced increase in extracellular ROS in neutrophils exposed to S. aureus (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: SLIT2-ROBO1 signaling robustly activates RhoA in macrophages and cancer cells.
source: We and others previously showed that SLIT2-ROBO1 signaling robustly activates RhoA, which in turn can activate Rho-associated protein kinases (ROCK), in several cell types, including macrophages and cancer cells (Bhosle et al., 2020; Kong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature including the authors' own work.

claim: In the presence of the selective ROCK inhibitor, Y-27632, N-SLIT2 failed to activate p38 MAPK in neutrophils.
source: We found that in the presence of the selective ROCK inhibitor, Y-27632, N-SLIT2 failed to activate p38 MAPK in neutrophils (Figure 2G–H).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: Exposure of blood to N-SLIT2 reduced neutrophil cell area and deformability although the effect did not reach statistical significance.
source: We performed Real-time deformability cytometry (RT-DC) and found that exposure of blood to N-SLIT2 reduced neutrophil cell area and deformability although the effect did not reach statistical significance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B; Bashant et al., 2019; Toepfner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Degranulation plays an important role in the bactericidal responses of neutrophils against S. aureus.
source: In addition to the oxidative burst, degranulation has been shown to play an important role in the bactericidal responses of neutrophils against S. aureus (Ferrante et al., 1989; Van Ziffle and Lowell, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Secondary and tertiary granules are most important for eliminating S. aureus.
source: Neutrophils contain four types of granules, each containing different classes of anti-microbial peptides, of which secondary and tertiary granules are most important for eliminating S. aureus (Borregaard and Cowland, 1997; Mollinedo, 2019; Van Ziffle and Lowell, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neither S. aureus alone nor S. aureus together with N-SLIT2 induced primary granule (CD63) secretion.
source: Neither S. aureus alone nor S. aureus together with N-SLIT2 induced primary granule (CD63) secretion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: S. aureus alone stimulated secondary granule (CD66b) exocytosis from neutrophils.
source: Congruent with published literature (Lu et al., 2014; Schmidt et al., 2012), the bacteria alone stimulated secondary granule (CD66b) exocytosis from neutrophils (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The effect of S. aureus on secondary granule exocytosis was strikingly enhanced by exposure to N-SLIT2.
source: This effect was strikingly enhanced by exposure to N-SLIT2 (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The actions of N-SLIT2 on secondary granule exocytosis were completely obliterated by pharmacological inhibition of p38 MAPK signaling using SB 203580 or p38 MAPK Inhibitor IV, but not MEK1/2 signaling using PD 184161.
source: Additionally, the actions of N-SLIT2 were completely obliterated by pharmacological inhibition of p38 MAPK signaling using SB 203580 or p38 MAPK Inhibitor IV, but not MEK1/2 signaling using PD 184161 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: N-SLIT2 augmented surface expression of S. aureus-induced CD18 in a p38 MAPK dependent manner.
source: It is noteworthy that N-SLIT2 also augmented surface expression of S. aureus-induced CD18, which is stored in both secondary and tertiary granules, in a p38 MAPK dependent manner (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E; Borregaard and Cowland, 1997; Mollinedo, 2019).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There were no differences in the surface expression of CD16 in any of the tested conditions.
source: On the other hand, we found no differences in the surface expression of CD16, which is stored in secretory vesicles, in any of the tested conditions, a finding in agreement with the priming-associated CD marker signature described for neutrophils in circulation and tissues (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F; Fine et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Exposure of blood to N-SLIT2 and S. aureus together significantly increased the fraction of primed neutrophils as compared to S. aureus alone.
source: Exposure of blood to N-SLIT2 and S. aureus together significantly increased the fraction of primed neutrophils as compared to S. aureus alone (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Incubation of human neutrophils with S. aureus resulted in the release of LL-37, which was further amplified in the presence of N-SLIT2 and blocked by the p38 inhibitors.
source: Incubation of human neutrophils with S. aureus resulted in the release of LL-37, which was further amplified in the presence of N-SLIT2 and blocked by the p38 inhibitors (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Exposure to N-SLIT2 alone failed to induce NETosis.
source: We investigated the effects of N-SLIT2 on NETosis and found that exposure to N-SLIT2 alone failed to induce NETosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H-J.

claim: Treatment of neutrophils with N-SLIT2 and S. aureus together resulted in more NETosis than that with the bacteria alone but this effect was not statistically significant.
source: Treatment of neutrophils with N-SLIT2 and S. aureus together resulted in more NETosis than that with the bacteria alone but this effect was not statistically significant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H–J).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H-J.

claim: Local SLIT2 levels were reduced as early as 12 hr after S. aureus infection.
source: Surprisingly, we found that local SLIT2 levels were reduced as early as 12 hr after the infection (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Following the initial decrease, the levels of SLIT2 gradually increased to reach a peak at 3 days after S. aureus infection.
source: Following the initial decrease, the levels of SLIT2 gradually increased to reach a peak at 3 days (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SLIT3 levels in the infected tissue remained significantly lower than in control mock-infected tissue for the first 2 days.
source: Unlike SLIT2, SLIT3 levels in the infected tissue remained significantly lower than in control mock-infected tissue for the first 2 days (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The bacterial counts were more than twofold higher in N-ROBO1-treated mice as compared to the IgG-treated counterparts.
source: Strikingly, the bacterial counts were more than twofold higher in N-ROBO1-treated mice as compared to the IgG-treated counterparts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In N-ROBO1-treated mice, S. aureus infection caused much more extensive tissue injury characterized by diffuse, rather than localized, inflammation.
source: In N-ROBO1-treated mice, S. aureus infection caused much more extensive tissue injury characterized by diffuse, rather than localized, inflammation (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-D.

claim: In the absence of bacterial infection, neutralization of endogenous SLIT2 augmented immune cell infiltration in the skin but did not result in local tissue damage in the form of acanthosis.
source: Interestingly, in the absence of bacterial infection, neutralization of endogenous SLIT2 augmented immune cell infiltration in the skin but did not result in local tissue damage in the form of acanthosis (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In the absence of SSTI, N-ROBO1 treatment alone was sufficient to increase neutrophil infiltration.
source: In the absence of SSTI, N-ROBO1 treatment alone was sufficient to increase neutrophil infiltration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Animals administered S. aureus and N-ROBO1 exhibited significantly more local neutrophil infiltration in infected tissue as compared to those administered S. aureus alone or S. aureus with control IgG.
source: In line with our earlier findings using H&E, animals administered S. aureus and N-ROBO1 exhibited significantly more local neutrophil infiltration in infected tissue as compared to those administered S. aureus alone or S. aureus with control IgG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: N-ROBO1-treated mice had an almost 50% reduction in the 8-OHdG-positive lesion area as compared to animals which received either S. aureus alone or S. aureus and control IgG.
source: N-ROBO1-treated mice had an almost 50% reduction in the 8-OHdG-positive lesion area as compared to animals which received either S. aureus alone or S. aureus and control IgG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F-G.

claim: Under specific non-infectious conditions, dermal microvascular endothelial cells (DMEC) and fibroblasts secrete SLIT2.
source: Under specific non-infectious conditions, dermal microvascular endothelial cells (DMEC) and fibroblasts have been previously reported to secrete SLIT2 (Pilling et al., 2014; Romano et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Infection of HMEC-1 with S. aureus was sufficient to reduce SLIT2 production at 12 hr at the level of mRNA as well as protein.
source: Infection of HMEC-1 with S. aureus was sufficient to reduce SLIT2 production at 12 hr at the level of mRNA as well as protein (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: The effect of S. aureus infection on SLIT2 production was reversed at 48 hr, at which time infected cells produced more SLIT2 than their non-infected counterparts.
source: However, the effect was reversed at 48 hr, at which time infected cells produced more SLIT2 than their non-infected counterparts (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Lowering the pH of the medium to 6.6 did not change SLIT2 mRNA in HMEC-1 cells.
source: Lowering the pH of the medium to 6.6 did not change SLIT2 mRNA in HMEC-1 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Growing HMEC-1 cells in a hypoxic (1% O2) environment replicated the effects of S. aureus infection on SLIT2 production.
source: In contrast, growing the cells in a hypoxic (1% O2) environment replicated the effects of S. aureus infection on SLIT2 production (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Conditioned media from HMEC-1 cells taken 48 hr after bacterial infection boosted LL-37 secretion and this effect was blocked by SLIT2 neutralization using N-ROBO1.
source: Conditioned media from HMEC-1 cells taken 48 hr after bacterial infection boosted LL-37 secretion and this effect was blocked by SLIT2 neutralization using N-ROBO1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Conditioned media from hypoxic HMEC-1 cells boosted LL-37 secretion and this effect was blocked by SLIT2 neutralization using N-ROBO1.
source: The same effect was also observed with conditioned media from hypoxic cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SLIT2 potentiates fMLP-induced oxidative burst in neutrophil-like HL-60 cells, without activating it on its own.
source: These findings are in keeping with those of Wu et al., who reported that SLIT2 potentiates fMLP-induced oxidative burst in neutrophil-like HL-60 cells, without activating it on its own (Wu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SLIT2-ROBO1 signaling inhibits macropinocytosis in macrophages in vitro as well as in vivo.
source: We recently reported that SLIT2-ROBO1 signaling inhibits macropinocytosis in macrophages in vitro as well as in vivo (Bhosle et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: N-SLIT2 does not affect FcγR-mediated phagocytosis of opsonized particles by neutrophils.
source: We show here that N-SLIT2 has no effect on phagocytosis of S. aureus by neutrophils and macrophages, in keeping with our previous observation that N-SLIT2 does not affect FcγR-mediated phagocytosis of opsonized particles by neutrophils (Chaturvedi et al., 2013), and an independent recent report showing that SLIT2 does not affect phagocytosis of M. tuberculosis by innate immune cells (Borbora et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: SLIT2 does not affect phagocytosis of M. tuberculosis by innate immune cells.
source: We show here that N-SLIT2 has no effect on phagocytosis of S. aureus by neutrophils and macrophages, in keeping with our previous observation that N-SLIT2 does not affect FcγR-mediated phagocytosis of opsonized particles by neutrophils (Chaturvedi et al., 2013), and an independent recent report showing that SLIT2 does not affect phagocytosis of M. tuberculosis by innate immune cells (Borbora et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The oxidative burst can be enhanced by priming agents, including tumor necrosis factor-α, which increase ROS production in response to secondary activating stimuli but have no effect on their own.
source: The oxidative burst can be further enhanced by priming agents, including tumor necrosis factor-α, which increase ROS production in response to secondary activating stimuli but have no effect on their own (Dang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In the resting state, three out of the five core components of the NOX complex, namely NCF1, NCF2, and NCF4, reside in the cytosol while the other two, CYBA and CYBB, are transmembrane proteins.
source: In the resting state, three out of the five core components of the NOX complex, namely NCF1, NCF2, and NCF4, reside in the cytosol while the other two, CYBA and CYBB, are transmembrane proteins (El-Benna et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The primed state of the NOX complex is characterized by phosphorylation of its cytosolic components, including NCF1, followed by their membrane translocation.
source: The primed state of the NOX complex is characterized by phosphorylation of its cytosolic components, including NCF1, followed by their membrane translocation (El-Benna et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: More than a dozen cellular protein kinases, including PKC and p38 MAPKs, have been implicated in NCF1 phosphorylation.
source: To date, more than a dozen cellular protein kinases, including PKC and p38 MAPKs, have been implicated in NCF1 phosphorylation (El-Benna et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The PKC-interacting protein AKAP79 binds to the C-termini of ROBO2/3, but fails to bind to the C-terminus of ROBO1.
source: These findings could be explained by the observation that in a cell-free system, the PKC-interacting protein AKAP79 binds to the C-termini of ROBO2/3, but fails to bind to the C-terminus of ROBO1 (Samelson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SLIT2 and its orthologues can stimulate p38 MAPK signaling in non-mammalian neurons.
source: Our studies revealed that N-SLIT2 induced p38 activation in human neutrophils and that inhibition of p38 signaling potently attenuated the observed N-SLIT2-mediated increase in oxidative burst. These results are in accordance with the observation that SLIT2 and its orthologues can stimulate p38 MAPK signaling in non-mammalian neurons (Campbell and Okamoto, 2013; Piper et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mice genetically overexpressing SLIT2 show hyperactivation of p38 MAPK.
source: Our results are also in agreement with a recent study reporting hyperactivation of p38 MAPK in mice genetically overexpressing SLIT2 (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: During the oxidative burst, PKC and p38 MAPK target distinct serine residues in the NCF1 C-terminus for phosphorylation.
source: Interestingly, during the oxidative burst, PKC and p38 MAPK target distinct serine residues in the NCF1 C-terminus for phosphorylation (Dang et al., 2006; Fontayne et al., 2002; Meijles et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SLIT2-induced p38 MAPK activation is not limited to innate immune cells.
source: Intriguingly, SLIT2-induced p38 MAPK activation is not limited to innate immune cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of findings in other cell types.

claim: N-SLIT2-ROBO1 signaling activates p38 in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cells as well as metastatic tumors.
source: Li et al. recently demonstrated that N-SLIT2-ROBO1 signaling similarly activates p38 in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cells as well as metastatic tumors but the underlying mechanism was not elucidated (Li et al., 2023b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SLIT2-induced modulation of Rho/ROCK signaling is vital for its effect on p38 MAPK activity.
source: Using a specific pharmacological inhibitor to disrupt cellular ROCK signaling (Y-27632), we show here that SLIT2-induced modulation of Rho/ROCK signaling is vital for its effect on p38 MAPK activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: Exposure to S. aureus increases CD66b surface levels in neutrophils.
source: Our results are congruent with previous reports that exposure to S. aureus increases CD66b surface levels in neutrophils (Mattsson et al., 2003), but we noted that this effect was further augmented by concurrent exposure to both N-SLIT2 and S. aureus.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Priming of the NOX complex by p38 MAPK results in the exocytosis of secondary granules in neutrophils.
source: This can be explained by our observation that N-SLIT2 activates p38 MAPK and primes the NOX complex. In neutrophils, priming of the NOX complex by p38 MAPK results in the exocytosis of secondary granules, and LL-37 is stored in its pro-peptide form in secondary granules (Potera et al., 2016; Sørensen et al., 1997; Ward et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: LL-37 is stored in its pro-peptide form in secondary granules.
source: This can be explained by our observation that N-SLIT2 activates p38 MAPK and primes the NOX complex. In neutrophils, priming of the NOX complex by p38 MAPK results in the exocytosis of secondary granules, and LL-37 is stored in its pro-peptide form in secondary granules (Potera et al., 2016; Sørensen et al., 1997; Ward et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neither S. aureus nor p38 activation induces primary granule release from neutrophils.
source: Our results are in line with studies showing that neither S. aureus nor p38 activation induces primary granule release from neutrophils (Lu et al., 2014; Potera et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: S. aureus induces NETosis in both a NOX-dependent and –independent manner.
source: S. aureus is known to induce NETosis in both a NOX-dependent and –independent manner (Douda et al., 2015; Parker et al., 2012; Pilsczek et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: S. aureus actively degrades NETs.
source: Additionally, S. aureus actively degrades NETs (Thammavongsa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A local reduction in SLIT3 mRNA levels was reported in patients after S. aureus-induced SSTI.
source: Congruent with our findings, a local reduction in SLIT3 mRNA levels was recently reported in patients after S. aureus-induced SSTI (Fyhrquist et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The neutralization of endogenous SLIT2 enhances macrophage macropinocytosis and inflammatory cytokine production in vivo in a peritonitis model.
source: These results are consistent with our previous observation that the neutralization of endogenous SLIT2 enhances macrophage macropinocytosis and inflammatory cytokine production in vivo in a peritonitis model (Bhosle et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: M. tuberculosis infection upregulates SLIT2 expression in macrophages in vivo and this is associated with increased ROS signaling.
source: Our results are also in accord with a recent report showing that M. tuberculosis infection upregulates SLIT2 expression in macrophages in vivo and this is associated with increased ROS signaling (Borbora et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Vascular endothelial cells are an important source of endogenous SLIT2 in vivo.
source: In recent years, vascular endothelial cells have emerged as an important source of endogenous SLIT2 in vivo (Romano et al., 2018; Tavora et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: miR-218 is differentially secreted in milk in a bovine model of S. aureus mammary infection.
source: It was recently reported that miR-218 is differentially secreted in milk in a bovine model of S. aureus mammary infection (Ma et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SLIT2 is a well-known host gene for miR-218 in vascular endothelial cells.
source: Since SLIT2 is a well-known host gene for miR-218 in vascular endothelial cells (Small et al., 2010), we asked whether DMEC, an endothelial cell type involved in SSTI, can secrete SLIT2 in response to S. aureus infection.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: S. aureus infection upregulates cellular hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1α) signaling in vitro as well as in vivo.
source: S. aureus infection is also known to upregulate cellular hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1α) signaling in vitro as well as in vivo (Werth et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HIF-1α negatively regulates SLIT2 expression in vascular smooth muscle cells.
source: Additionally, Li et al., very recently reported that HIF-1α negatively regulates SLIT2 expression in vascular smooth muscle cells (Li et al., 2023a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: S. aureus- and/or hypoxia-induced early upregulation of HIF-1α in DMEC could directly suppress SLIT2 production.
source: These findings have important implications for S. aureus-induced SSTI. First, S. aureus- and/or hypoxia-induced early upregulation of HIF-1α in DMEC could directly suppress SLIT2 production.
evidence: This is an inference based on the integration of findings from the current study and prior literature.

claim: The rapid initial decrease in SLIT2 (and SLIT3) at the site of infection may serve to augment the immediate recruitment of neutrophils to combat the infection.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that host-derived SLIT2 plays an important role in the spatiotemporal modulation of innate immune responses during bacterial infection. The rapid initial decrease in SLIT2 (and SLIT3) at the site of infection may serve to augment the immediate recruitment of neutrophils to combat the infection, while the rise in SLIT2 several days later may promote localized retention of recruited neutrophils and enhancement of their bactericidal properties.
evidence: This is an inference based on the integration of experimental findings and known functions of SLIT2.

claim: The rise in SLIT2 several days after infection may promote localized retention of recruited neutrophils and enhancement of their bactericidal properties.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that host-derived SLIT2 plays an important role in the spatiotemporal modulation of innate immune responses during bacterial infection. The rapid initial decrease in SLIT2 (and SLIT3) at the site of infection may serve to augment the immediate recruitment of neutrophils to combat the infection, while the rise in SLIT2 several days later may promote localized retention of recruited neutrophils and enhancement of their bactericidal properties.
evidence: This is an inference based on the integration of experimental findings and known functions of SLIT2.

claim: Spatiotemporal regulation of SLIT2/ROBO1 activity may potently direct bacterial killing and confer effective host protection against pathogenic infection.
source: In this manner, spatiotemporal regulation of SLIT2/ROBO1 activity may potently direct bacterial killing and confer effective host protection against pathogenic infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the integration of experimental findings.

claim: SLIT2 could serve as a therapeutic to combat S. aureus and could have broader anti-microbial activity against a number of pathogens including Mycobacterium tuberculosis, intestinal pathogens, H5N1 influenza, and SARS-CoV-2.
source: Recent studies by independent research groups suggest that SLIT2 could not only serve as a therapeutic to combat S. aureus, but could have broader anti-microbial activity against a number of pathogens including Mycobacterium tuberculosis, intestinal pathogens, H5N1 influenza, and SARS-CoV-2 (Borbora et al., 2023; Gustafson et al., 2022; London et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and represents speculation about therapeutic potential.

claim: SLIT2 may represent an attractive alternative or synergistic therapeutic strategy given mounting concerns about the growing resistance of bacterial pathogens to conventional pharmacologic antibiotic treatment.
source: Given mounting concerns about the growing resistance of bacterial pathogens to conventional pharmacologic antibiotic treatment, SLIT2 may represent an attractive alternative or synergistic therapeutic strategy.
evidence: This is speculation about the therapeutic potential of SLIT2.
